newsitem.title: USA: U.S. regulators voice concern over consumer debt.
newsitem.headline: U.S. regulators voice concern over consumer debt.

text.p: Key banking regulators voiced concern on Thursday about the recent steep rise in consumer debt but said it did not pose a threat to the economic recovery or the health of the U.S. banking system.
"The level of debt and the fact that debt has been growing so quickly is a matter of grave concern," Federal Reserve Gov. Lawrence Lindsey told the House Banking Committee.
But, he added, "We do not believe that current debt levels pose a threat to the continuation of the present economic expansion."
The job market is "quite good" and consumer confidence is high, he said.
The steep rise in consumer debt -- particularly credit card debt -- has helped fuel a continued climb in consumer spending during the current 5-1/2 year-old expansion.
It has also led to increased delinquencies on consumer loans and additional personal bankruptcies.
U.S. Comptroller of the Currency Eugene Ludwig echoed Lindsey's concern about the the steep rise in consumer debt and about the worsening credit quality of consumer loans.

"We are concerned about the high levels of debt held by cosumers today," he told lawmakers. "These high levels leave many consumers, and therefore the banks that lend to them, vulnerable to financial shocks."
But Ludwig, whose office oversees some of the nation's largest banks, said the problem was not widespread enough to pose a threat to the health of the banking system as a whole.
"The condition of the banking system is strong," he said. "The nation's banks have recorded four consecutive years of record profits."
Lindsey urged banks to take a "prudent look" at their loan portfolios but he was opposed to regulatory or legislative action to force banks to cut back on their consumer loans.
"I couldn't imagine any more effective way of causing a recession than to do that," he said.
While consumers were spending freely, the Fed has to be careful, Lindsey said.
"On the one hand, it's our objective to make sure that we have a stabilising role in the economy, that any downturn not be a severe one," he said.

"On the other hand, there's the proverbial 'take away the punch bowl' role (for the Fed)," he said. "One might conclude that when you're spending an extra $1.10 for every dollar you're getting in a raise, that maybe a few people have had a nip or two too much."
